hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.regret_scenario: 12 months out: ~30 µservices each emit audit seals with subtly different discipline. Cross-µservice seal-chain integrity is unverifiable because no lane CI-enforced it. A compliance audit asks 'show me every state-changing inter-µservice call seals to audit-chain' and we cannot answer.
hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.mitigation: BLOCK promotion of any µservice past dev until oya-check-audit-chain-seal-coverage lane exists AND is wired into oya-dev-cli gate dispatcher. ADR-0145 should not be Accepted without its enforcement primitives existing — currently it is an aspirational ADR.

Each new µservice-to-µservice edge requires hand-written Cedar policy fragments + review. hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.title: ADR-0145 'cell-µservice load grows' but cell capacity-model NOT updated for new mTLS handshake rate

hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.regret_scenario: Production traffic ramps. SPIRE server hits its SVID-issuance ceiling because cell capacity-model was sized for edge-ingress-only, not full sibling-µservice mesh. hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.title: ADR-0145 cargo-cults AWS Step Functions without acknowledging Step Functions provides cross-µservice transaction semantics direct-gRPC does NOT
evidence: ADR-0145 §Alternatives D: 'Pure hyperscaler shape with 3 weaker invariants (accepted) ... matches AWS / Google / Microsoft / Stripe / Anthropic shape'
AWS Step Functions provides: distributed-transaction sagas, durable retry, compensation, exactly-once semantics, exponential backoff with jitter. Direct gRPC provides NONE of these.

ADR-0145 names 'Workflow MAY be used for durable long-running cross-µservice orchestration (sagas, retry-with-backoff, human-in-the-loop, multi-step transactions)' — but this is OPT-IN. There's no rule for WHEN a µservice MUST use Workflow vs direct gRPC.
Without a 'when to use Workflow' rubric, engineers will default to direct gRPC for everything, then debug saga-like failures via custom code, badly.
hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.regret_scenario: Month 6: an inter-µservice flow needs to update 3 entities atomically. Engineer uses direct gRPC, hand-rolls retry, gets it subtly wrong, leaks half-committed state. The org rediscovers Saga pattern via prod incident. Workflow exists but no one knew when to reach for it.
hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.mitigation: Add ADR-0146 'When-to-use-Workflow rubric' OR a Consequences section in ADR-0145 enumerating the 4-5 patterns that MUST use Workflow (multi-µservice state mutations, human-in-the-loop, long-running with retries > 30s, etc.).

hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.title: Ontology as 'preferred path for cross-µservice entity reads where latency budget permits' is unmeasurable
evidence: ADR-0145 §Decision/Invariant 3: 'Ontology query is the preferred path for cross-µservice entity reads where latency budget permits.'
What's the latency budget threshold? Not specified. Engineers will route around Ontology citing 'latency' without proof, eroding the substrate's value over time.
Compare: Palantir Foundry's Ontology has SLO-typed read paths with documented p99 budgets. Our ADR-0145 has no analogous specification.
hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.regret_scenario: Ontology becomes vestigial: engineers default to direct gRPC because 'Ontology is too slow' (assertion, not measurement). Cross-µservice queryability drifts; we have 30 sets of canonical entity contracts.
hunt_1_adr_0145_meta_regrets.mitigation: Add per-Ontology-axis p99 read budget (e.g., 50ms hot, 200ms cold) and require an ADR to bypass it. Forces measurement before bypass.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: oya-dev-cli is a monolith dispatcher (single-process, single-crate) for 52+ gates — anti-hyperscaler shape
evidence: crates/oya-dev-cli/src/commands/gate/mod.rs uses a single `match (verb, lane)` arm-list to dispatch ALL gates.
Adding a new gate (e.g., oya-check-eu-ai-act-annex-iii-refusal) requires touching this central mod.rs.
This is the SAME anti-pattern Workflow+Ontology had: a single central authority that must be modified for every µservice change.
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS uses per-tool CLIs (aws s3, aws iam, aws lambda) with separate code paths; not one monolithic dispatcher.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: AWS Tools / Google Cloud SDK / Azure CLI all use plugin architectures where each service registers via a discovery mechanism, not a hand-edited central dispatcher. Our oya-dev-cli is the architectural antipattern we just retired.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Phase 1 (M02): convert oya-dev-cli to plugin-registry where each oya-check-* crate registers a CommandSpec via inventory or linkme. Phase 2 (M03): split into oya-dev-cli (orchestrator) + per-axis CLIs (oya-governance-cli, oya-foundry-cli).

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: Single audit-chain µservice instance — not sharded per-tenant or per-cell
evidence: microservices/audit-chain/ shows a single µservice with single Helm chart. Not sharded.
ADR-0145 makes EVERY state-changing inter-µservice call emit a seal to audit-chain. Volume grows multiplicatively.

Compared to: AWS CloudTrail (per-account isolation), Azure Monitor (per-workspace), GCP Cloud Audit Logs (per-project) — all enforce hard per-tenant boundaries to prevent cross-tenant volume contamination AND for sovereignty.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: Hyperscalers shard audit at tenant/project boundary. Our single audit-chain creates a noisy-neighbor risk: one chatty tenant degrades the seal-write SLO for all tenants. Also: data sovereignty becomes hard (EU tenant + US tenant audit data co-mingled).
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: ADR-0146 'audit-chain per-cell shardability': document per-cell audit-chain deployment topology; the audit-chain seal storage shards by (cell, tenant); cross-cell verification is via Merkle-tree root commitment, not by querying a single store.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: Centralized Cedar policy evaluation — single OpenBao/PDP per cell rather than cell-local PEP+PDP
evidence: microservices/governance/policy/ structure suggests centralized policy authoring. Per-call evaluation path not clearly cell-local.
ADR-0145 §Decision says 'Cedar policy authorization (per-call)' — but doesn't specify WHERE the PDP runs.
If Cedar PDP is in oya-governance-cedar µservice, every inter-µservice call routes through it — re-creating the ESB-2.0 anti-pattern in the authz layer.
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS IAM evaluates entirely cell-local via in-process IAM SDK. No round-trip to central IAM service per call.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: AWS IAM, Google Cloud IAM, Azure RBAC: in-process policy evaluation via SDK with pre-distributed policy bundles. Round-trip to PDP for every call would 10x the latency budget. Cedar is designed for cell-local PEP+PDP, but our deployment topology isn't specified.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Author ADR for 'Cedar policy distribution topology': PDP-as-sidecar OR PDP-as-library, with policy-bundle propagation via OpenBao. Forbid central-PDP roundtrip for hot-path authz.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: Single canonical Helm helpers library (Helm umbrella in microservices/observability) shared across 33 µservices
evidence: Helm template `include "oya.networkPolicy.allowEgressToCarriers" $` referenced in microservices/network/iac/helm/network/templates/networkpolicy.yaml + meet — implies a shared _helpers.tpl library.
If a single helpers library, then a breaking change ripples across 33 µservices simultaneously.
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS CDK has per-construct libraries with semver; not one monolithic helpers file shared by everyone.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: Per-axis Helm helper libraries with semver pinning is the production shape (compare: aws-cdk-lib L1/L2 split, Pulumi providers). Our single helpers.tpl couples 33 µservices to one library version.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Split helpers.tpl into per-axis libraries (oya.network.tpl, oya.observability.tpl) under microservices/<axis>/iac/helm-helpers/. µservices import explicitly via Helm dependencies.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: Synchronous audit-chain seal — no read-your-writes invariant nor async path documented
evidence: ADR-0145 §Decision/Invariant 1: 'Every state-changing inter-µservice call MUST emit an audit-chain seal at the calling service'.
Synchronous emission means audit-chain availability sits in the critical path of every state-changing call. Audit-chain outage → every write-path fails.
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS CloudTrail uses async fire-and-forget with delivery guarantees via S3 + retries. The control-plane writes don't block on CloudTrail.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: CloudTrail / Azure Audit Logs / GCP Audit Logs: async with bounded retry. The audit emission is on critical path for legal reasons but the latency is async-batched, not sync-blocking.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Document the sync-vs-async seal path in ADR-0145 OR a successor ADR. Default async with local WAL + delivery worker. Synchronous only for HIPAA/Sox-Article-6 paths. Make read-your-writes the explicit contract via a per-µservice WAL.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: 33-µservice list as a known-set (hardcoded list) — not a dynamic registry
evidence: microservices/ directory enumerates a known list; the count appears in PRDs, evidence, and review scripts as a hardcoded number.
Adding the 34th µservice requires touching multiple registries by hand.
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS services are discovered via service-discovery; not enumerated in a static list.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: Service registries (Consul, etcd, ServiceCatalog) provide dynamic enumeration. Our static directory + static count couples authoring tooling to one specific topology.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Author a dynamic registry under registry/microservices/index.json that's auto-generated from microservices/*/manifest.json. Forbid hardcoded 33-count anywhere.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: manifest.json regenerated by single generator — single point of failure for cross-µservice catalog truth
evidence: PR #143 mentions 'Fix-B's generator fix' regenerated manifest.json files. If a single generator owns this, then ALL µservices share that generator's defect surface.
Hyperscaler comparison: each AWS service ships its own service-spec definition; AWS does NOT have a single generator authoring all 200+ service catalogs.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: Per-µservice ownership of manifest is the hyperscaler shape. A single generator violates Conway's law and creates a coupling chokepoint.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: Convert generator into a per-µservice lint that VALIDATES manifest.json against schema, but each µservice owns the authoring.

hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.title: 11-pack overlay as ahead-of-time set rather than runtime jurisdiction resolution
evidence: PRD wording suggests packs are pre-enumerated (KR, US-Healthcare, EU-GDPR, etc.).
Hyperscaler comparison: AWS Region availability is runtime-resolved per request; tenant jurisdiction → applicable region → applicable compliance overlay is a runtime resolution, not a fixed set.
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.anti_hyperscaler_comparison: Compliance overlays as runtime jurisdiction graphs allow per-request policy resolution. Pre-enumerated packs become brittle as jurisdictions multiply (Canada PIPEDA, Brazil LGPD, India DPDPA, China PIPL coming).
hunt_2_other_anti_hyperscaler_patterns.migration_path: M03 or later: refactor packs to a jurisdiction graph (region → applicable_overlays []) with runtime resolution.

hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.title: Service-mesh sprawl: ADR-0145 enables N² mTLS handshakes without specifying service-mesh tooling
evidence: ADR-0145 §Decision/Direct sibling-µservice egress: 'NetworkPolicy egress rules MAY allow direct egress to sibling µservices gRPC endpoints, subject to mTLS authentication ...'
No mention of Istio / Linkerd / Cilium / AWS App Mesh. No service-mesh choice committed.
33 µservices × O(N) sibling edges = up to 528 mTLS handshakes worth of cert management. Without a mesh, this is hand-rolled.
Hyperscaler comparison: at this density, every hyperscaler uses a mesh (Stripe → Twirp + custom mesh; Google → Stubby + global service-discovery; AWS → App Mesh / VPC Lattice).
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.regret_scenario: By month 9, cert-rotation incidents cascade weekly. Manual SPIFFE-ID issuance scripts can't keep up. We retroactively adopt Istio under incident pressure with no design budget.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.mitigation: Author ADR-0147 'service-mesh decision' (Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium vs custom Tower interceptor library). Pre-condition direct sibling-µservice egress on the mesh ADR landing.

hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.title: Distributed audit-chain emission has NO cross-service causality contract
evidence: ADR-0145 §Decision/Invariant 1: 'Every state-changing inter-µservice call MUST emit an audit-chain seal at the calling service'.

If µservice A calls µservice B which calls µservice C, who seals what? Each one seals its own call independently. The CROSS-FLOW causal chain (A→B→C) is reconstructed only via OTel tracing, not via the seal-chain.
Compare to old Workflow+Ontology rule: the Workflow event-bus naturally provided a causal chain because every flow had a single root event.
Cross-µservice forensic reconstruction (legal subpoena, breach investigation) becomes harder.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.regret_scenario: An audit query asks 'show me every operation that touched user X' — answer requires joining 33 µservice seal logs by trace-id, hoping every µservice honored OTel propagation. One µservice with bad OTel propagation = broken causality chain.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.mitigation: Add Invariant 4 to ADR-0145: 'every audit-chain seal MUST include the OTel trace-id + parent-span-id; cross-µservice causality is reconstructable from (trace-id, seal-timestamp).' Validate via 'oya-check-audit-seal-trace-binding' lane.

hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.title: Ontology becomes single point of contention if all 33 µservices write to it
evidence: ADR-0145 §Decision/Invariant 3: 'µservices that own canonical entities MUST project them into Ontology.'
30+ µservices projecting writes into Ontology = write-hot-spot.
No mention of Ontology partition strategy. Single Ontology µservice serializes every projection write.
Palantir Ontology in production is partitioned by tenant + entity-type — not a single-database design.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.regret_scenario: Ontology projection lag grows with µservice count. Cross-µservice entity reads become stale by minutes. Engineers route around Ontology because freshness budget exceeded; substrate erodes.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.mitigation: Author Ontology partitioning ADR. Per-tenant + per-entity-class sharding with projection-lag SLO.

hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.title: Cedar per-call authz latency budget never specified — risk of N² authz traffic
evidence: ADR-0145 §Direct egress: 'Cedar policy authorization (per-call)' — but no latency budget.
33 µservices × O(N) sibling calls × Cedar eval = up to 528 Cedar eval edges. At 10ms each = 5.3s additional latency budget overhead in a worst-case 528-hop trace.
Without a budget, engineers will treat Cedar as 'free' and chain calls, then debug latency cascades.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.regret_scenario: P99 latency budgets blow up in month 6. Profiler shows Cedar eval as top time sink. We adopt Cedar caching under duress, with cache-invalidation correctness bugs.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.mitigation: Specify Cedar eval budget per inter-µservice call (e.g., <1ms p99 via in-process PDP + 1s policy bundle freshness). Require ADR-0148 'Cedar PDP topology + caching contract'.

hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.title: Direct µservice-to-µservice contracts grow without versioning discipline
evidence: ADR-0145 §Consequences/Negative #3: 'Per-µservice contract surface grows — each µservice's contracts/openapi or contracts/proto carries the surfaces siblings call.'
No mention of contract-versioning lane (Buf breaking-change detection, OpenAPI semver enforcement).

Old rule: Workflow events carried versioned contracts via single registry. New rule: 33 µservices × N siblings × per-edge contract = combinatorial contract surface with no central versioning authority.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.regret_scenario: Month 8: µservice A removes a proto field. Two sibling µservices break in prod simultaneously. No CI lane caught the breaking change because contracts/proto/*.proto was edited without a buf-breaking check.
hunt_6_reform_new_regrets.mitigation: Add 'oya-check-proto-breaking' lane (Buf breaking-change detection) AND 'oya-check-openapi-breaking' lane (oasdiff). Pre-condition ADR-0145 ramp.
